name: Sumdog
line: Sumdog places with a test, then practice runs in games. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Sumdog: Sumdog places with a diagnostic test, then practice runs in games. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Sumdog places a child with a diagnostic test at first login, then sets math questions inside games, pitched to the level the test found [2][3]. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Sumdog starts with a diagnostic test at first login, in two parts that can run over several sessions, and pitches its game questions to the level the test finds [3][2].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, each problem carries what a learner needs: a hint that gives the first step and never the answer, a written lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer after it is answered, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Sumdog the unit is the game. Questions come inside games, and right answers earn coins for avatar costumes and a virtual house [2][7][9]. Its math page describes games and questions, and no lessons, hints or worked examples [2]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve math performance, mostly on researchers' own tests [14].

reasons.title: The adult's part
reasons.body: In AMP the adult does not plan, teach or grade. Parents and teachers see a level for each part of math and the actual problems behind every number, and each lesson has a guide for the adult. In Sumdog, teachers assign tasks on specific skills or let the questions adjust on their own [4], and parents can set work and monitor progress [5].

reasons.title: From counting through precalculus
reasons.body: AMP is one program from counting through precalculus, on one map of skills. It keeps a separate level for each part of math, so a learner further along in one part than another gets work at both levels, and repeated misses send practice back to what a skill builds on. Sumdog is built for ages 5 to 14 [1], and its fluency program covers kindergarten to grade 5 [8].

theirs: Sumdog is game-based practice in math, and in spelling and grammar, for ages 5 to 14 [1]. On first login a child starts a diagnostic test in two parts, which can run over several sessions [3]. After that the child plays math games, with questions pitched to the level the test found [2]. Right answers earn coins for avatar costumes and a virtual house [7][9].

In schools, teachers assign tasks on specific skills or let the questions adjust on their own [4], and classes can enter weekly contests with questions drawn from each student's diagnostic [6]. Sumdog also offers fluency practice: Fluency Booster for kindergarten to grade 5 [8], and a times-tables check with a time limit [7].
credit: A diagnostic places each child before practice begins [3].
Regular fact-fluency practice, including a timed times-tables check [7][8].
The What Works Clearinghouse rates regular timed fluency activities as strong evidence for elementary students who struggle in math [12].

theirs: Sumdog's about page cites an "independent study in Glasgow" and says 30 minutes a week almost doubles a child's fluency progress [10]. The page names no researchers, design, sample or effect size and gives no reference, so we could not check it. Its math, fluency, times-tables and contest pages cite no other study [2][8][7][6].
We found no entry for Sumdog in the Evidence for ESSA search [11]. The pages we read link no outcome study of Sumdog.
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Worked examples improve mathematics performance, with an average effect of g = 0.48 across 55 studies, mostly on researchers' own tests [14]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed, spaced practice scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks, on the researchers' own test a month later [13]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You want timed fact-fluency practice inside games for a child in the early grades.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or past age 14.
You want printed practice made from your child's own record, with worked answer keys.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Sumdog?
questions.answer: Sumdog places a child with a diagnostic test, then sets questions inside games at that level [2][3]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem in that part of math, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Sumdog work?
questions.answer: Its about page cites a study in Glasgow but gives no reference [10]. We found no entry for Sumdog in the Evidence for ESSA search [11]. The pages we read link no outcome study.

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers and chooses practice from there.
